Trump voters' remorse: what's the real number? A new Navigator poll says 18 percent of Trump voters in 2024 regret their vote. But that's not the politically meaningful number: only 8 percent are willing to change their vote. That's about 3.5 percent of all voters, which isn't small in the American system but is far less than the headline suggests. The erosion is from the margins of the coalition, not its core. Among Republicans, only 9 percent of MAGA are remorseful, versus 24 percent of non-MAGA and 22 percent of younger voters. The reason for the remorse is also clear: unfulfilled promises (30 percent), war and foreign policy (27 percent), and the cost of living (25 percent). In the closed-ended question, 45 percent directly named the war with Iran. A more interesting point: in this same sample, Trump voters who are not remorseful have a positive economic assessment. Two groups in a single economy report two completely opposite economic experiences. Economic perception is a function of political identity, not merely of prices.@sadegh_alhosseini

Is the dollar expensive or cheap today?
Sadegh Al-Hosseini
This chart shows the dollar exchange rate at today's prices; that is, each past rate has been adjusted for Iran's inflation so it can be compared with today's money. The result is:
• The peak of Mehr and Aban 1397: about 19 thousand tomans, equivalent to 455 thousand tomans today
• In 1399: the rate was about 25 thousand tomans, equivalent to 300 thousand tomans today
• Esfand 1401: the rate of 53 thousand tomans, equivalent to 241 thousand tomans today
So today's dollar, in real terms, is about half the peak of 1397 and roughly at the same level as Esfand 1401 and Khordad 1398. What has happened in these years is mostly the collapse of the rial's value rather than a real rise in the dollar's price. So what matters is the growth of liquidity, not even sanctions and siege!
Big nominal numbers deceive us; the only correct measure is the inflation-adjusted rate.
Important point: the real rate being low compared to historical peaks does not mean the dollar will remain cheap in the future. That is, the recent nominal jumps have only compensated for accumulated inflation, not gone beyond it.
@sadegh_alhosseini

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @sadegh_alhosseini

The hidden shock absorber of the oil market in this war was China's reserves. Before the war, Beijing had stockpiled about 1.4 billion barrels. When Hormuz was closed, it cut its purchases to a ten-year low and drew down its reserves; that very absence neutralized part of the price shock. Now the tables have turned: August imports reached 8.93 million barrels per day, and Shanghai oil is trading at a premium above Brent. But this is not a recovery in consumption; China's gasoline and diesel consumption is still 8 and 9 percent below last year. China is buying oil to fill its reserves, and it knows this decline in consumption is not permanent either. That is, China has gone from being a price brake to a gas pedal. Until yesterday, its absence kept prices in check; today, its presence pushes them up, and the cost of prolonging the war comes out of Beijing's pocket—and that just two weeks before Xi's trip to Washington. But China's mediation has always been low-risk; it steps in when an agreement is almost ripe, and Trump is not one to commit to any lasting deal. Beijing has found an incentive to end this war, but it issues the bill in the name of Washington and Tehran.@sadegh_alhosseini
